classification.difficultyReason: Connect a change-of-base proof with a decreasing logarithmic graph and two dilations on shared axes.

inlines.text: Use the change-of-base formula to show that
, and hence sketch these graphs on one set of axes:

answer.short:
$\log_{1/3}x=\dfrac{\log_3x}{-1}=-\log_3x$.

All three curves decrease, with domain $x>0$, range $\mathbb R$ and vertical asymptote $x=0$. The first two cross at $(1,0)$; the third crosses at $(\tfrac12,0)$. See the shared sketch.
answer.worked:
For $x>0$,
$$\begin{align*}\log_{1/3}x&=\frac{\log_3x}{\log_3(1/3)}\\\log_{1/3}x&=\frac{\log_3x}{\log_3(3^{-1})}\\\log_{1/3}x&=\frac{\log_3x}{-1}\\\log_{1/3}x&=-\log_3x.\end{align*}$$
Reflect $y=\log_3x$ in the $x$-axis. The resulting curve $y=\log_{1/3}x$ passes through $(\tfrac13,1)$, $(1,0)$ and $(3,-1)$.

Dilate this curve vertically by factor $2$ to obtain $y=2\log_{1/3}x$, passing through $(\tfrac13,2)$, $(1,0)$ and $(3,-2)$.

Dilate the original curve horizontally by factor $\tfrac12$ to obtain $y=\log_{1/3}(2x)$, passing through $(\tfrac16,1)$, $(\tfrac12,0)$ and $(\tfrac32,-1)$.

Draw all three decreasing curves on the same axes. Each approaches $+\infty$ as $x\to0^+$ and $-\infty$ as $x\to\infty$; the $y$-axis is their common vertical asymptote.

spec.description: Equation-driven shared sketch with three decreasing logarithmic curves. A separate legend distinguishes solid, dashed and dotted curves without crowding their branches.
spec.mathematics: Solid: -ln(x)/ln(3); dashed: -2ln(x)/ln(3); dotted: -ln(2x)/ln(3). Common vertical asymptote x=0. Intercepts 1, 1 and 1/2 respectively.
